title: Leaked Biden Tapes: Classified Info and Memory Lapses Surface from Pre-Presidency Interviews
summary: In a dramatic disclosure, a conservative activist group has released roughly three hours of audio tapes in which former Vice President Joe Biden appears to share classified information with his memoir ghostwriter—and at times admits to memory lapses. The recordings, made in 2016 and 2017 before Biden's presidency, were obtained by the Oversight Project, an arm of the Heritage Foundation, after a protracted legal fight. The tapes capture Biden speaking with author Mark Lewis Zwonitzer. In one 2017 session, Biden says, "I just found all the classified stuff downstairs," and proceeds to describe a handwritten 40-page memo he sent to President Obama arguing against a troop surge in Afghanistan. The specific classified content is redacted, but the context suggests Biden retained sensitive materials after leaving office. The release revives a contentious chapter: Special Counsel Robert Hur investigated Biden's handling of classified documents and, in 2024, declined to prosecute. Hur noted that a jury might view Biden as a "sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory"—a characterization that ignited fierce debate over Biden's fitness for office. The tapes contain moments where Biden cannot recall dates or details, yet he also demonstrates a command of many foreign policy discussions. The Oversight Project's vice president of litigation, Jeff Clark, claimed the tapes "prove Biden's decline" and belong to the American people. Biden's spokesman, TJ Ducklo, blasted the release as "politically motivated" and an abuse of power, asserting the conversations were private and shared with the Justice Department on condition of confidentiality. Biden initially sued to block disclosure but dropped the case after a divided appeals court ruled there was a "substantial" public interest. The tapes now fuel ongoing questions about transparency, age, and the handling of classified information at the highest levels of government.
why_it_matters: The leaked tapes raise uncomfortable questions about how much trust the public can place in leaders whose private records show both deep knowledge and troubling forgetfulness, and they test the boundaries between privacy and accountability in an aging political class.

background_read: Joe Biden served as the 46th U.S. president from 2021 to 2025; before that, he was vice president under Barack Obama (2009–2017). The leaked recordings come from before his presidency, when he was a private citizen working on a memoir.
Mark Lewis Zwonitzer was the ghostwriter hired to help Biden tell his life story, and their conversations included both policy discussions and personal reflections.

Special Counsel Robert Hur, appointed to investigate Biden’s handling of classified documents, found evidence that sensitive materials had been improperly stored but concluded that a jury would likely see Biden as a forgetful, well‑meaning elderly man—a statement that set off a political firestorm.

The Heritage Foundation is a conservative think tank that uses litigation and public campaigns to push right‑leaning policy; its Oversight Project specializes in obtaining government records through legal battles.
Jeff Clark, the Oversight Project’s vice president who pronounced the tapes proof of Biden’s decline, was previously a Trump‑era Justice Department official who promoted claims of election fraud.

perspectives.description: Biden’s defenders argue the tapes actually show him recalling complex foreign policy arguments, proving he remained sharp. They view the leak as a partisan weapon from a conservative group, timed to damage his reputation, and stress that he shared the materials with the Justice Department voluntarily.

Critics see the tapes as evidence that Biden mishandled classified material and that his memory lapses confirm the Hur report’s unflattering portrait. Even if no charges were filed, they contend the public deserves to know about the judgment and mental acuity of someone who held the highest office.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical – Confidentiality vs. public interest
perspectives.description: The case highlights a recurring tension: confidential conversations with ghostwriters often sit in gray areas of record‑keeping law. The appeals court’s ruling that public interest outweighed privacy sets a precedent that may affect future memoirs and the handling of sensitive notes by top officials.

The leak could lead to stricter rules requiring former officials to immediately hand over all written and recorded materials. It may also intensify calls for age limits or cognitive tests for presidential candidates, reshaping how the country selects its leaders.
